subtype: Approach: reading the timetable and packing the night before [Action]
passage: I'm Aditi, and Amandeep lives in the flat below mine, so I see a lot of him. Around seven every evening his window is open and I can see him at the study table. He pulls tomorrow's timetable off the wall, reads it with his finger, then tips out the day's books. Maths and Hindi go back on the shelf; science and the drawing notebook slide in. Last come the lunch box, rinsed and dry, and the steel water bottle. In the morning I hear no shouting from his house at all. He walks out with his bag already on, humming, while I am still hunting for a sock.

qa.q: What goes into Amandeep's bag after the science and drawing notebooks?
qa.a: The lunch box and the steel water bottle go in last.

qa.q: What might Amandeep be feeling as he walks out humming?
qa.a: He seems calm and content; humming and a bag already on his back show no rush or worry.

qa.q: What other approach could help someone whose mornings are rushed, and why?
qa.a: Aditi could copy the evening packing, because choosing books without a clock ticking removes the scramble. A short list checked at the door could also catch forgotten things.

qa.q: How does Amandeep's routine look from Aditi's side of the wall?
qa.a: Aditi is still hunting for a sock while he is ready to go, so it likely looks like a calm, sensible habit that Aditi could learn from.

grounding: An evening timetable check and packing of the right books, lunch and water leads to a calm morning, seen by a neighbour.

subtype: Approach: using a coloured chart pinned on the wall [Action]
passage:
Hrithik: Didi, why is the wall covered in colours?
Amandeep: It's my week chart. Blue is maths, green is science, orange is Hindi, pink is drawing.
Hrithik: Tuesday is nearly all green!
Amandeep: Science and its practical file are both on Tuesday. First I ruled the days, then I coloured the boxes, then Papa helped me pin it up. Now I glance once and I know which books go in.
Hrithik: Can I make one, chhote bhai style?
Amandeep: You are the chhote bhai. Take the markers. What do you colour first?
Hrithik: Sports, in red!
Amandeep: Good. Yours goes lower on the wall, where you can reach.

qa.q: Which colour stands for science on Amandeep's chart?
qa.a: Green is science.

qa.q: What does Hrithik seem to want when Hrithik asks to make a chart too?
qa.a: Hrithik wants a chart like Amandeep's; the eager questions and choosing red for sports show real interest.

qa.q: What other approach could help Hrithik get the bag right, and why?
qa.a: Hrithik could read the timetable in the evening and pack the night before, because a calm check at home means fewer mistakes in the morning. A short list at the door could also work.

qa.q: How might Papa see the colour chart on the wall?
qa.a: Papa probably sees a sensible habit; Papa helped pin it up and is likely happy for both children to have one.

grounding: A girl colours each subject on a weekly chart pinned on the wall so the day's books are clear at a glance.

subtype: Approach: throwing everything in the bag just in case [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Hemant, and I sit next to Gurpreet in Class 6. He never checks the timetable; every book he owns goes into the bag, every day. By the second period he was leaning forward like an old man, and on the stairs he held the railing. Then the teacher asked for the English notebook. He dug past the atlas, the drawing file and a spare geometry box, pulling out crumpled sheets before he found it. The whole class waited, and he went red. At lunch he rubbed his shoulder, and when the strap slipped I saw the red marks.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet dig past before he found the English notebook?
qa.a: He dug past the atlas, the drawing file and a spare geometry box.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt while the whole class waited?
qa.a: Embarrassed; he went red while everyone watched him search. 😔

qa.q: What other approach could Gurpreet try, and why would it work better?
qa.a: He could read the timetable and pack only tomorrow's books, since a light bag is easier to carry and a neat bag is easier to search. A short checklist at the door would also help.

qa.q: How does Hemant see Gurpreet's habit?
qa.a: Hemant sees a plan that costs Gurpreet comfort and time, and seems concerned rather than mocking, since he notices the strap marks and how the class waited.

grounding: A child keeps every book in the bag to avoid checking the timetable, and it becomes heavy and messy so the notebook is still hard to find.

subtype: Approach: checking the bag against a short list at the door [Thinking]
passage:
Before the first bell in Class 5, Farida opened her diary and copied five words on the last page: homework, lunch, bottle, pencil box, diary. Thomas, at the next desk, leaned over. "You never forget anything."
"I do when I'm in a hurry," Farida said. "Yesterday Ammi was calling me for the bus and my head went empty. I left my bottle on the table."
"So the list is for the door?"
"Yes. My memory is bad at that time, but a pencil tick doesn't panic. I'll check each thing, one by one." She underlined homework twice. Thomas laughed and copied the idea for himself.

qa.q: What five things did Farida write on the last page of her diary?
qa.a: She wrote homework, lunch, bottle, pencil box and diary.

qa.q: What is Farida worried about when she is in a hurry?
qa.a: She worries that her head goes empty when she is rushed, like the day she left her bottle on the table.

qa.q: What other approach could help Farida, and why?
qa.a: Farida could read the timetable and pack the night before, because a calm evening check leaves less to remember in the morning rush. Keeping things in fixed places could also help.

qa.q: How does Thomas see Farida's list?
qa.a: Thomas finds it sensible enough to copy for himself, so to him it looks like a useful trick and not a weakness.

grounding: A girl writes a short list of five school items and ticks it at the door because she cannot trust her memory when rushed.

subtype: Approach: putting things back in the same place each day [Thinking]
passage: The bell for maths rang and thirty bags unzipped at once. Pema, at the next desk, was already pulling out books, a pencil case, a sticky water bottle, half a packet of biscuits. Lokesh did not look down. His hand slid into the front pocket and came back with the geometry box. "How do you always find it so fast?" Pema whispered. "It lives there," Lokesh whispered back. "Front pocket, box. Back pocket, diary. I decided in Class 5 and never changed it." He thought: if it goes back in the same spot, my hand will know without my head. Pema found her compass under the biscuits and groaned.

qa.q: Where does Lokesh keep his diary?
qa.a: His diary lives in the back pocket.

qa.q: What does Lokesh think about putting things back in the same spot?
qa.a: He thinks his hand will know where things are without his head having to remember, which shows he trusts the habit.

qa.q: What other approach could Pema try, and why?
qa.a: Pema could empty her bag and pack it again with a fixed place for each item, since a steady spot saves searching. Checking the bag against a short list at the door could also help.

qa.q: How does the routine look to Pema, who is digging under the biscuits?
qa.a: Pema sees how easy it is for Lokesh and feels a little annoyed at her own mess; the whisper and groan suggest she wants to learn his trick.

grounding: A boy assigns fixed pockets for his geometry box and diary so he need not search when the bell rings.

subtype: Approach: forgetting the change of timetable for PT day [Pitfall]
passage: Vidhi packed her bag on Tuesday night the way she had for weeks, from memory. She never noticed that the timetable had changed and Wednesday now began with PT. At school there was no time to fix anything: the whole class lined up on the ground right after prayers, and the bell would not wait. "Where are your white shoes?" the PT teacher asked. Vidhi looked down at her black school shoes. "At home," she said quietly. She spent the period on a bench under the neem tree. Saurabh waved from the game, and she waved back but her chin stayed low.

qa.q: Where did Vidhi spend the PT period?
qa.a: She sat on a bench under the neem tree.

qa.q: What does Vidhi's low chin suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she is embarrassed and disappointed at missing the game, even though she waved back at Saurabh.

qa.q: What other approach could Vidhi try, and why would it help?
qa.a: Vidhi could check the timetable on the wall or a written copy on Sunday and Tuesday night, because packing from a current list catches changes that memory misses.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Vidhi's mistake?
qa.a: Saurabh probably sees a friend left out of the game; his wave shows he cares and might want her to join if she could.

grounding: A girl packs from memory of last week's plan, forgets the new PT day and cannot play without her white shoes.

subtype: Approach: adding a note about changes to the plan [Revision]
passage:
Chandrika: Chetta, look at the chart. See the yellow square on Wednesday?
Jomon: A note that says PT shoes. Why the note?
Chandrika: Last week I sat out PT. The timetable had changed and my chart still showed the old one. I felt so silly on that bench.
Jomon: So the note will fix it?
Chandrika: The note is for Wednesday. But changes can come any week, so on Sunday evenings I read the school diary before I pack.
Jomon: And if the note falls off?
Chandrika: Then the Sunday check catches it. Two ways, so I won't get caught again.
Jomon: Smart plan, little sister. I will ask you before my next test.

qa.q: What does the note on Chandrika's chart say?
qa.a: The note says PT shoes, and it sits on the Wednesday square.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel when sitting out PT last week?
qa.a: Chandrika felt silly and disappointed, which is why the mistake must not happen again.

qa.q: What other approach could Chandrika use, and why?
qa.a: Chandrika could ask a classmate to tell Chandrika about timetable changes, since a friend may hear news first. A short list at the door could also catch missing items.

qa.q: How does Jomon see the plan?
qa.a: Jomon finds it smart; asking what happens if the note falls off shows Jomon is testing the plan and is happy to see two ways to catch a change.

grounding: After the PT shoe mistake, Chandrika adds a note to the chart and reads the diary on Sundays for changes.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent to pack it for him [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday night. Akash's mother packed his bag as always, humming while he watched television. Akash never looked at what went in.

Wednesday night. Mummy left for a cousin's wedding in another town. "Pack your own bag, beta," she said on the phone. Akash stared at the timetable and could not tell which day it was for.

Thursday. He reached school with the Hindi reader, the wrong maths book and no drawing file. Tanvir shared his book in maths, but the teacher wrote a remark in the diary, and Akash sat out drawing with an empty page.

qa.q: Why did Akash's mother leave on Wednesday night?
qa.a: She left for a cousin's wedding in another town.

qa.q: What was Akash probably feeling when he stared at the timetable on Wednesday night?
qa.a: He was likely confused and a little anxious, because he never watched what went in and could not tell which day it was for.

qa.q: What other approach could Akash try, and why?
qa.a: Akash could learn to read the timetable and pack with his mother watching a few times, so he is ready when she is away. A list on the wall could also guide him.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Akash's wrong books?
qa.a: Tanvir was willing to share his book, which suggests he sees a classmate in trouble and wants to help him get through the lesson.

grounding: A boy who lets his mother pack every night cannot manage when she is away and arrives with the wrong books.

subtype: Approach: sorting loose papers into a folder each Friday [Action]
passage: Esha's school in the village ended at one o'clock, but on Fridays she stayed on the verandah with her bag. She tipped everything onto the floor: pencil shavings, a torn worksheet, three balled-up sheets from art, a notice about the fair. The crumpled ones went into the tin bin. The notice and worksheets she smoothed and slid into a blue plastic folder that her uncle had bought from the shop at the bus stand. Jatin watched from the steps. "Why so slow?" he asked. "Because in Week Three the fair notice will be in here, not lost," Esha said. Three weeks later, she found it at once.

qa.q: What colour is the plastic folder Esha uses?
qa.a: The folder is blue.

qa.q: What might Esha be feeling when she finds the fair notice at once three weeks later?
qa.a: She probably feels pleased and relieved, because her Friday habit worked and the notice was not lost. 😊

qa.q: What other approach could help Esha keep her papers safe, and why?
qa.a: Esha could ask a teacher or parent to show her how to organise them, or she could write down notices in a notebook. Either way she would keep track of what matters.

qa.q: How does Jatin see Esha's Friday work?
qa.a: Jatin thinks it looks slow, since he asks why she takes so long, but he watches closely and may learn from the result.

grounding: A girl empties her bag every Friday, bins crumpled papers and files notices in a folder, so fewer papers get lost over the weeks.

subtype: Approach: making a guest list with a limit on numbers [Thinking]
passage:
Shankar: Mummy, I want the whole class at my party. That's thirty-four.
Mummy: The flat holds fifteen, my clever boy, counting cousins.
Shankar: Fifteen. Hmm. Let me write. Cousins first: Gurpreet, Neha, Ravi, Kabir. Four. Then friends I play with every day. Eight, nine... nineteen in all.
Mummy: That is four too many.
Shankar: I know. If I cut the ones I only sit near in class, those are four names. The people who matter most stay. It feels bad, but nobody can come to a cramped party anyway.
Gurpreet: Am I in?
Shankar: You're the first one on the list.

qa.q: How many people can the flat hold for the party?
qa.a: The flat holds fifteen, counting cousins.

qa.q: How does Shankar feel about cutting names from the list?
qa.a: Shankar feels bad about it, but accepts it because a cramped party would not be fun for anyone.

qa.q: What other approach could Shankar try, and why?
qa.a: Shankar could ask if the whole class could join a small outing later, since more friends can be included without crowding the flat. Sharing a treat at school could also work.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel when asking whether an invitation is coming?
qa.a: Gurpreet is probably nervous and hopeful, since Gurpreet asks aloud and is glad to hear the name is first on the list.

grounding: A boy whose parents can host fifteen counts the names, puts cousins and close friends first and cuts a few.
